claim: Direct monitoring of mosquito populations in field settings is a crucial input for shaping appropriate and timely control measures for mosquito-borne diseases.
source: The direct monitoring of mosquito populations in field settings is a crucial input for shaping appropriate and timely control measures for mosquito-borne diseases.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of mosquito monitoring for disease control, drawing on established knowledge in public health and vector control.

claim: Commercially available mobile phones are capable of acoustically mapping mosquito species distributions worldwide.
source: Here, we demonstrate that commercially available mobile phones are a powerful tool for acoustically mapping mosquito species distributions worldwide.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and field demonstrations presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Low-cost mobile phones with very basic functionality are capable of sensitively acquiring acoustic data on species-specific mosquito wingbeat sounds.
source: We show that even low-cost mobile phones with very basic functionality are capable of sensitively acquiring acoustic data on species-specific mosquito wingbeat sounds, while simultaneously recording the time and location of the human-mosquito encounter.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with the 2006 Samsung SGH T-209 feature phone and other low-cost devices.

claim: Mobile phones simultaneously record the time and location of human-mosquito encounters.
source: We show that even low-cost mobile phones with very basic functionality are capable of sensitively acquiring acoustic data on species-specific mosquito wingbeat sounds, while simultaneously recording the time and location of the human-mosquito encounter.
evidence: This is a known capability of mobile phones with GPS and timestamping features.

claim: Acoustic recordings supported by spatio-temporal metadata enable rapid, non-invasive species identification.
source: We survey a wide range of medically important mosquito species, to quantitatively demonstrate how acoustic recordings supported by spatio-temporal metadata enable rapid, non-invasive species identification.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the classification experiments and field trials presented in the manuscript.

claim: Minimally-trained users can map local mosquitoes using their personal phones.
source: As proof-of-concept, we carry out field demonstrations where minimally-trained users map local mosquitoes using their personal phones.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the field trials at Big Basin Redwoods State Park and Ranomafana, Madagascar.

claim: There is a paucity of high-resolution ecological data on the abundance, temporal variation, and spatial distribution of mosquito vector species.
source: However, there is a paucity of high-resolution ecological data on the abundance, temporal variation, and spatial distribution of mosquito vector species.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of mosquito surveillance as documented in the literature.

claim: The paucity of ecological data poses a serious impediment to the effective control of mosquito-borne diseases.
source: This poses a serious impediment to the effective control of mosquito-borne diseases (Townson et al., 2005; Ferguson et al., 2010; Hay et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on mosquito control challenges.

claim: Efforts to map mosquito populations primarily rely on interpolative mathematical models based on factors such as clinical disease burdens or climatological data.
source: Efforts to map mosquito populations primarily rely on interpolative mathematical models based on factors such as clinical disease burdens or climatological data, with field inputs from entomological surveys being a comparatively sparse contribution (Hay et al., 2010; Mordecai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work on mosquito mapping methodologies.

claim: Field inputs from entomological surveys are a comparatively sparse contribution to mosquito mapping efforts.
source: Efforts to map mosquito populations primarily rely on interpolative mathematical models based on factors such as clinical disease burdens or climatological data, with field inputs from entomological surveys being a comparatively sparse contribution (Hay et al., 2010; Mordecai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on mosquito surveillance methods.

claim: The scarcity of field data stems from the absence of high-throughput, low-cost surveillance techniques to map the distribution of mosquitoes.
source: This scarcity of field data stems from the absence of high-throughput, low-cost surveillance techniques to map the distribution of mosquitoes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current state of mosquito surveillance technology and practices.

claim: Currently used methods like trapping and manual identification require considerable expense, labour, and time.
source: This effect is particularly severe in resource-constrained areas, as currently used methods like trapping and manual identification require considerable expense, labour, and time.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about traditional mosquito surveillance methods.

claim: Acoustic surveillance was proposed decades ago as a high-throughput automated surveillance approach.
source: Acoustic surveillance was proposed decades ago as a high-throughput automated surveillance approach, where mosquitoes in flight are identified using the species-specific frequencies in their wingbeat sounds (Kahn et al., 1945; Kahn and Offenhauser, 1949a; Offenhauser and Kahn, 1949; Kahn and Offenhauser, 1949b; Jones, 1964; Johnson and Ritchie, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple historical citations to early work on acoustic mosquito surveillance.

claim: Acoustic surveillance identifies mosquitoes in flight using species-specific frequencies in their wingbeat sounds.
source: Acoustic surveillance was proposed decades ago as a high-throughput automated surveillance approach, where mosquitoes in flight are identified using the species-specific frequencies in their wingbeat sounds (Kahn et al., 1945; Kahn and Offenhauser, 1949a; Offenhauser and Kahn, 1949; Kahn and Offenhauser, 1949b; Jones, 1964; Johnson and Ritchie, 2016).
evidence: This is the fundamental principle of acoustic surveillance, supported by citations to historical literature.

claim: Sexual selection has led to characteristic sound signatures for different mosquito species.
source: This technique is based on the hypothesis that sexual selection has led to characteristic sound signatures for different mosquito species (Roth, 1948; Belton, 1994; Gibson and Russell, 2006; Cator et al., 2009; Warren et al., 2009; Pennetier et al., 2010; Cator et al., 2010).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by multiple citations to published research on mosquito acoustic behavior.

claim: The challenge of using expensive microphones to acquire low amplitude mosquito sounds against potentially high background noise poses a significant barrier to widespread adoption of acoustic surveillance as a field technique.
source: However, the challenge of using expensive microphones to acquire low amplitude mosquito sounds against potentially high background noise poses a significant barrier to its widespread adoption as a field technique (Jones, 1964; Unwin and Ellington, 1979; Raman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature discussing technical challenges in acoustic mosquito surveillance.

claim: Around 5.3 billion users worldwide are connected by the global mobile network.
source: Further, the proliferation of the global mobile network implies that around 5.3 billion users worldwide are connected today by a distributed data transmission infrastructure, growing quickly at over 6% annually (Cerwall et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a factual statistic cited from a published report on mobile network usage.

claim: The global mobile network is growing at over 6% annually.
source: Further, the proliferation of the global mobile network implies that around 5.3 billion users worldwide are connected today by a distributed data transmission infrastructure, growing quickly at over 6% annually (Cerwall et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a factual statistic cited from a published report on mobile network growth.

claim: The explosive growth in mobile phone use is most pronounced in Africa, Asia, and Latin America.
source: Also, the explosive growth in mobile phone use is most pronounced in Africa, Asia, and Latin America (Cerwall et al., 2017), which also bear the brunt of mosquito-borne diseases (World Health Organization, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to reports on mobile phone adoption and disease burden.

claim: Africa, Asia, and Latin America bear the brunt of mosquito-borne diseases.
source: Also, the explosive growth in mobile phone use is most pronounced in Africa, Asia, and Latin America (Cerwall et al., 2017), which also bear the brunt of mosquito-borne diseases (World Health Organization, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a WHO report on disease burden.

claim: Mobile phones record species-specific wingbeat sounds from mosquito vector species for automated identification and analysis.
source: We use the sensitive microphones in mobile handsets to record species-specific wingbeat sounds from a variety of mosquito vector species for automated identification and analysis (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is the core methodology demonstrated throughout the manuscript with experimental data.

claim: Mobile phones are optimized for sophisticated audio capture, processing, and transmission.
source: Our technique exploits the rapid advances in mobile phone hardware technology, recognizing that these highly portable devices are optimized for sophisticated audio capture, processing, and transmission.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about mobile phone technology and design.

claim: Mosquito sounds have relatively low complexity, comprising a single fundamental frequency with several overtones.
source: Mosquito sounds have relatively low complexity. They comprise a single fundamental frequency with several overtones, which we identify using the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) (Figure 1C, Video 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated through spectral analysis of mosquito sounds shown in the figures.

claim: The sound from typical flight traces is not monotone, but shows natural frequency variations captured as a wingbeat frequency distribution.
source: The sound from typical flight traces is not monotone, but shows natural frequency variations which we capture as a wingbeat frequency distribution, in a range characteristic of the given species (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through the frequency distribution analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Sexual dimorphism in most mosquito species implies that males have higher wingbeat frequencies than females.
source: Sexual dimorphism in most species implies that males have higher frequencies than females.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about mosquito acoustic biology.

claim: Female mosquito wingbeat frequencies are typically between 200 and 700 Hz.
source: Female wingbeat frequencies are typically between 200 and 700 Hz.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the experimental data collected from 20 mosquito species.

claim: Female mosquito wingbeat frequencies overlap the voice frequency band (300 to 3000 Hz), in which phones are designed to have maximum sensitivity.
source: This overlaps the voice frequency band (300 to 3000 Hz), in which phones are designed to have maximum sensitivity.
evidence: This combines data on mosquito frequencies with knowledge about phone microphone design.

claim: Mobile phone microphones accurately capture wingbeat frequencies without distortion.
source: Our concept of mobile phone based acoustic surveillance is based on the idea that mobile phones are high fidelity acoustic sensors, which faithfully capture the frequencies produced by mosquito wingbeats during flight.
evidence: This is validated through comparison with high-speed video measurements.

claim: Spectrograms from synchronized audio-video recordings of tethered Culex tarsalis mosquitoes were aligned in time to within 2 ms and show an exact match in frequency at each time window to within 2 Hz.
source: For synchronized audio-video recordings, spectrograms were aligned in time to within 2 ms, and show an exact match in frequency at each time window to within a computational error margin of 2 Hz (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through the synchronized audio-video experiment with tethered mosquitoes.

claim: Wingbeat frequency distributions from video and audio have a Bhattacharya Coefficient of 0.95, indicating almost complete overlap.
source: We obtain a high BC of 0.95, implying an almost complete overlap between the distributions.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data comparing video and audio measurements.

claim: Both smartphones and low-end feature phones have SNRs comparable to reference microphones over distances up to 100 mm.
source: Using a piezoelectric buzzer of constant amplitude (77 dB at source) and frequency (500 Hz) as a standardized sound source, we first showed that both smartphones (iPhone 4S, Xperia Z3 Compact) and low-end feature phones (Samsung SGH T-209 clamshell model) have SNRs comparable to the reference microphones over distances up to 100 mm (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through calibration experiments with standardized sound sources.

claim: All phones tested, including a decade-old basic phone (SGH T-209), are capable of acquiring detectable wingbeat sound up to 50 mm from a mosquito.
source: Curves of mobile phone SNR over distance indicate that all the phones tested, including a decade-old basic phone (SGH T-209), are capable of acquiring detectable wingbeat sound up to 50 mm from a mosquito (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through distance calibration experiments with tethered mosquitoes.

claim: Smartphones like the Xperia can acquire mosquito sound at distances up to 100 mm.
source: This distance improves to 100 mm in the case of smartphones like the Xperia, making it even easier for users to record mosquito sound (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through distance calibration experiments with the Xperia smartphone.

claim: Working distance limits for mobile phone mosquito recording are appropriate in quiet to moderately noisy environments with background noise levels below 50 dB.
source: We also caution that these working limits are appropriate in quiet to moderately noisy environments with background noise levels below 50 dB, and shrink drastically in louder conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the signal-to-noise ratio measurements and acoustic principles.

claim: Eight different smart and feature phones ranging in price between ~$20 and ~$700 recorded quantitatively equivalent acoustic data from Anopheles stephensi mosquitoes.
source: We compared eight different smart and feature phones ranging in price between ~$20 and ~$700 (Figure 2F), by analyzing 5 minutes of audio recorded with each phone from free-flying female Anopheles stephensi mosquitoes of similar age from a lab-reared population contained in a cage.
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparative recordings from multiple phone models.

claim: Mean and median frequencies obtained by each phone differed by less than 5% from other phones for the same mosquito population.
source: We noted high degrees of overlap in wingbeat frequency distributions recorded by each phone for this population, with both mean and median frequencies obtained by each phone differing by less than 5% from other phones (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is calculated from the comparative data across different phone models.

claim: The Bhattacharya Coefficient between phone pairs for the same mosquito population ranged between 0.93 and 1, indicating high degrees of overlap.
source: We computed the Bhattacharya Coefficient (BC) and obtained high degrees of overlap between 0.93 and 1 (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is calculated from the frequency distributions recorded by different phones.

claim: The Jensen-Shannon divergence for each pair of phones had low values below 0.3, indicating high similarity in measurement.
source: The JSD for each pair of phones had low values below 0.3 indicating high similarity in measurement, corroborating that wingbeat frequency sampling is relatively insensitive to the phone used.
evidence: This is calculated from the frequency distributions recorded by different phones.

claim: A diverse range of both smart and feature phones provide highly similar acoustic spectra from the same population of mosquitoes.
source: Thus, we demonstrate that a diverse range of both smart and feature phones provide highly similar acoustic spectra from the same population of mosquitoes, enabling a truly universal acoustics-based platform for mosquito identification.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the comparative analysis of recordings from multiple phone models.

claim: Representative populations from 20 medically relevant mosquito species were surveyed under similar experimental conditions to establish a reference dataset.
source: We surveyed representative populations from 20 medically relevant mosquito species under similar experimental conditions (Figure 3A), to establish a reference dataset for classifying acoustic recordings (Mukundarajan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is the experimental dataset collected and presented in the manuscript.

claim: A basic low-end phone (SGH T-209) is capable of collecting high-quality acoustic recordings to precisely measure wingbeat frequency distributions.
source: Although we recorded mosquitoes using a variety of phones, the results presented here focus on data acquired by the 2006-model $20 SGH T-209 feature phone. This highlights that even a basic low-end phone is capable of collecting high-quality acoustic recordings, to precisely measure wingbeat frequency distributions.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the reference dataset collected using the T-209 phone.

claim: A typical wingbeat frequency distribution for any given species has a spread of 150 to 200 Hz between the 5th and 95th percentiles.
source: A typical wingbeat frequency distribution for any given species has a spread of 150 to 200 Hz between the 5th and 95th percentiles, located within the frequency range of 200 to 700 Hz for most female mosquitoes.
evidence: This is observed from the frequency distribution data collected from 20 mosquito species.

claim: Approximately 60 samples, or 1.2 seconds of recording time, is sufficient to generate a well-sampled wingbeat frequency distribution for a given population.
source: The time for convergence above a BC of 0.9 corresponds to approximately 60 samples, or 1.2 seconds of recording time, to generate a well-sampled wingbeat frequency distribution for a given population.
evidence: This is calculated from the convergence analysis of bootstrapped subsets from reference distributions.

claim: Different lab-reared strains of Anopheles gambiae produced highly similar frequency distributions with mutual Bhattacharya Coefficients of 0.84 to 0.89.
source: We found that different lab-reared strains of An. gambiae, including permethrin susceptible and resistant variants sourced from Kenya and an additional bendiocarb resistant strain sourced from Benin, produced highly similar frequency distributions with large overlaps of 0.84 to 0.89 as measured by their mutual BCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparative analysis of different An. gambiae strains.

claim: Different colonies of Aedes aegypti had high overlaps in their frequency distributions with mutual Bhattacharya Coefficients ranging between 0.66 and 0.74.
source: Similarly for Aedes aegypti, lab-reared mosquitoes from two separate colonies of the same New Orleans origin, as well as first generation progeny from eggs retrieved from the field in Los Angeles, had high overlaps in their frequency distributions with mutual BCs ranging between 0.66 and 0.74 (the slightly lower BC values arise due to the distribution for one of the colonies having a smaller spread despite being completely overlapped by the other two) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparative analysis of different Ae. aegypti colonies.

claim: Lab-reared strains of Anopheles arabiensis from Senegal and Sudan have non-overlapping frequency distributions with a Bhattacharya Coefficient of 0.14.
source: However, we also found that lab-reared strains of An. arabiensis originally sourced from Senegal and Sudan have non-overlapping frequency distributions, with a very small BC of 0.14 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparative analysis of different An. arabiensis strains.

claim: The vast majority of all possible pairwise combinations of species (184 out of 190) had Jensen-Shannon divergence greater than 0.35.
source: The vast majority of all possible pairwise combinations of species in our study (184 out of 190) had JSD greater than this minimum value (Figure 3B), indicating that differences in frequency distribution between species are significant in most cases (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is calculated from the pairwise comparisons of frequency distributions for 20 species.

claim: Species with fairly unique and non-overlapping wingbeat frequency distributions are almost always correctly classified.
source: Our results verify that species with fairly unique and non-overlapping wingbeat frequency distributions are almost always correctly classified, while those with high degrees of overlap are most likely to be mutually misclassified.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the confusion matrix analysis of bootstrapped data.

claim: Including a location filter based on entomological survey data significantly improved classification accuracy from about 35% to 65% on average.
source: This significantly improved classification accuracy not only for individual species, but also from about 35% to 65%, as an average over all the species tested (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through the classification experiments with and without location filtering.

claim: Anopheles gambiae and Culex pipiens can easily be distinguished by sound alone with negligible probability of mutual mis-classification.
source: In the simplest case, species with completely non-overlapping frequency distributions, such as Anopheles gambiae and Culex pipiens (JSD = 1, negligible probability of mutual mis-classification), can easily be distinguished by sound alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through the frequency distribution analysis and classification results.

claim: Anopheles gambiae and Anopheles quadriannulatus are correctly identified with over 97% probability.
source: The JSD for all but one species pair ranges between 0.61 and 0.91 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E), and An. gambiae and An. quadriannulatus are correctly identified with over 97% probability.
evidence: This is calculated from the classification analysis of the An. gambiae species complex.

claim: Mosquito recordings with high SNR were obtained in a wide range of ambient environments, from urban and rural homes to forests and parks.
source: We also collected recordings in a wide range of ambient environments, from urban and rural homes, both indoors and outdoors, to forests and parks (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary files 2–7). We obtained mosquito recordings with high SNR, whose distinctive narrow-spectrum characteristics allow their easy visual identification in spectrograms against background noises such as birdsong, fire truck sirens, and human speech.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the field recordings collected in various environments.

claim: For individual flight traces collected in the field, the frequency distributions have spreads between 10 and 100 Hz.
source: For individual flight traces collected in the field, the distributions lie at different positions within the population-level frequency range, and have spreads (difference between 5th and 95th percentile) between 10 and 100 Hz (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is observed from the analysis of individual Aedes sierrensis recordings from the field.

claim: The spread in frequency for a single flight trace is typically smaller than the spread across a population.
source: The spread in frequency for a single flight trace is typically smaller than the spread across a population, with the difference between mean frequencies for different traces contributing to the additional variation in the population's frequency distribution.
evidence: This is observed from the comparative analysis of individual traces versus population distributions.

claim: Frequency distributions for individual flight traces have a minimum spread of around 2% of the mean frequency irrespective of the mean frequency or the duration of the recording.
source: We also observed that frequency distributions for individual flight traces have a minimum spread of around 2% of the mean frequency irrespective of the mean frequency or the duration of the recording, suggesting that this is an inherent natural variation in the wingbeat frequency during free flight (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is observed from the analysis of individual flight traces from wild Aedes sierrensis.

claim: For mosquitoes varying almost two-fold in size, the difference in mean frequency between each mosquito is less than the spread within each individual flight trace.
source: For mosquitoes varying almost two-fold in size (Figure 3G), the difference in mean frequency between each mosquito is less than the spread within each individual flight trace, and non-monotonic with body size (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through the analysis of Aedes sierrensis specimens with varying body sizes.

claim: The MLE approach correctly classified recordings from wild Aedes sierrensis mosquitoes in about two-thirds of cases (54 out of 82 recordings).
source: Despite the variations among individuals, our MLE approach (using a pool of all field recordings together to create a reference frequency distribution) was able to correctly classify recordings from wild Aedes sierrensis mosquitoes in about two-thirds of cases (54 out of 82 recordings), when considering other local species (Cx. pipiens, Cx. quinquefasciatus, Cx. tarsalis, and Cu. incidens) as potential confounders.
evidence: This is calculated from the classification analysis of field recordings from Big Basin Park.

claim: Recordings from Big Basin Redwoods State Park were collected over a continuous 3 hour period by 15 volunteers hiking along trails and recording with their personal mobile phones.
source: These were collected over a continuous 3 hour period by 15 volunteers hiking along trails and recording with their personal mobile phones.
evidence: This describes the field trial methodology at Big Basin Park.

claim: About 60 recordings were collected in a 3-hour period by 10 volunteers at Ranomafana, Madagascar.
source: About 60 recordings were collected in a 3-hour period by 10 volunteers who were trained for about 15 minutes and stationed at specific locations in the village.
evidence: This describes the field trial methodology at Ranomafana.

claim: The number of recordings at Ranomafana exceeded the number of mosquitoes simultaneously captured in CDC light traps placed at the same locations.
source: This number of recordings exceeded the number of mosquitoes simultaneously captured in CDC light traps placed at the same locations.
evidence: This is a direct comparison between mobile phone recordings and traditional trapping methods.

claim: CDC light traps collected Anopheles mosquitoes only in those locations where they were also recorded by volunteers.
source: This heterogeneity was concordant with the data from CDC light traps, which collected Anopheles mosquitoes only in those locations where they were also recorded by volunteers (Figure 4C, insets).
evidence: This is observed from the comparison of mobile phone recordings and trap data at Ranomafana.

claim: Wingbeat frequency for insects, including mosquitoes, has been shown to vary linearly with temperature.
source: Wingbeat frequency for insects, including mosquitoes, has been shown to vary linearly with temperature (Oertli, 1989; Villarreal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from published literature on insect flight physiology.

claim: Lab studies show no relationship between wingbeat frequency and body size.
source: This provides a field confirmation of lab studies that show no relationship between wingbeat frequency and body size (Villarreal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from published literature and confirmed by field observations in this study.
